title: Theory of Constraints
subtitle: Find the one thing slowing everything else down and fix that first
useWhen: You are optimising multiple parts of your business simultaneously but overall performance is not improving proportionally. You're busy improving things that don't move the needle because the real bottleneck is somewhere else.
howToUse: Eliyahu Goldratt introduced the Theory of Constraints in his 1984 novel The Goal. The core insight is that every system has exactly one constraint at any given time the bottleneck that limits overall throughput. Improving anything that is not the constraint does not improve the system. The Five Focusing Steps are: Identify the constraint, Exploit it (get maximum output from it without major investment), Subordinate everything else (optimise the system to support the constraint), Elevate it (invest to increase its capacity), and Repeat (once solved, find the next constraint).
steps: Map your entire delivery process and find where work piles up that is your constraint.
The constraint is almost never where you think it is - it is where queue builds up, not where people are busiest.
Before investing in fixing the constraint, exploit it first, squeeze maximum output from what you have.

Once one constraint is resolved, immediately identify the next, constraints shift as systems improve. Solving the constraint isn't the finish line it's the start of finding the next one. Founders who fix one bottleneck and stop optimizing are surprised when a new one appears; it was always there, just hidden behind the first.
origin: Eliyahu Goldratt, The Goal, 1984 — Theory of Constraints

proTip:
The most counterintuitive TOC insight is that making a non-constraint more efficient
makes the constraint worse. If your constraint is sales and you invest in a faster delivery
team, you now have an even more frustrated delivery team waiting for work. Fix the
constraint first. Everything else is noise until you do.
